contentMarkdown:
To convert HEIC to JPG on iPhone, you don't need to install an app or pay for a converter. Open a free converter in Safari, pick the HEIC photo from your camera roll, and download the JPG in under a minute — the file never leaves your phone. This guide covers the browser method, the camera setting that stops HEIC photos, the Photos app export trick, and the Mac method for batches — plus what to do when a file won't convert.

![An iPhone held in hand — photos taken on iPhone save as HEIC by default](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1512941937669-90a1b58e7e9c?w=1200&q=80)

## Why your iPhone saves photos as HEIC

Since iOS 11, iPhones save photos in HEIC (High Efficiency Image Container) by default. It stores the same quality in roughly half the file size of JPG, which is why Apple made it the default. The catch is compatibility: many Windows apps, websites, job portals, government forms, and older devices simply can't open HEIC files. So the photo looks perfect on your iPhone and fails everywhere else — which is exactly why converting HEIC to JPG on iPhone is one of the most searched iPhone fixes.

You have two choices: convert the photos you already have, or change the camera setting so new photos save as JPG. Both are covered below, and both are free.

## Method 1: Convert HEIC to JPG in Safari — free, no app

This is the most direct option, and it works on any iPhone running a modern version of iOS. No app to install, no account to create.

1. Open the [free HEIC to JPG converter](/tools/heic-to-jpg-converter) in Safari.
2. Tap to browse your files and pick the HEIC photo from your Photos library or the Files app.
3. Leave the quality slider at its default of 92% — visually identical to the original at a much smaller file size.
4. Tap "Convert to JPG" and save the result.

The converted JPG lands in the Files app under Downloads. From there you can share it anywhere: WhatsApp, email, a job portal, a print shop — JPG opens everywhere.

Because the conversion runs entirely in your browser with the heic2any engine, your photo is never uploaded to a server. That matters for personal photos: upload-based converters keep a copy on someone else's machine, even briefly. Here, nothing leaves your phone.

Converting several photos? Do them one at a time — the converter handles one file per run, and a fresh page load between files keeps Safari's memory use low.

## Method 2: Stop your iPhone taking HEIC photos

If you're tired of converting every photo, change the camera format once and every new photo saves as JPG from then on:

1. Open **Settings** and tap **Camera**.
2. Tap **Formats**.
3. Switch from **High Efficiency** to **Most Compatible**.

From now on, new photos save as JPG and new videos as the widely compatible MP4 format. Your existing HEIC photos stay as HEIC — this only changes what the camera captures next — so use Method 1 for the photos already in your library.

The trade-off is honest: JPG files are bigger than HEIC, so photos take up more storage. On a 128 GB iPhone that rarely matters; on a 64 GB phone that's nearly full, it's worth knowing. You can switch back to High Efficiency any time.

## Method 3: Export JPGs from the Photos app

Your iPhone already converts HEIC to JPG in some situations automatically — and you can use that:

- **Sharing to apps that don't support HEIC:** when you share a photo from the Photos app to an app that can't handle HEIC, iOS converts it to JPG on the way out. This is why a photo emailed from your iPhone usually arrives as a JPG.
- **Transferring to a computer:** in **Settings → Photos → Transfer to Mac or PC**, choose **Automatic**. When you plug your iPhone into a Windows PC and copy photos over, they arrive as JPG instead of HEIC.

Neither of these helps when a website's upload form rejects your HEIC file directly from Safari — for that, Method 1 is the reliable route.

## Method 4: Convert a batch on Mac with Preview

If you have a Mac and a folder of HEIC photos to convert, Preview does it offline with no extra software:

1. Select the HEIC files in Finder and open them in Preview (double-click, or right-click → Open With → Preview).
2. Select all the images in the sidebar (Cmd + A).
3. Go to **File → Export Selected Images**.
4. Choose **JPEG** as the format, pick a quality, and choose a folder.

Preview converts the whole batch at once. For one or two photos, the Safari method is faster; for dozens, this is the better tool.

## What quality should you pick?

The converter's quality slider runs from 10% to 100% and defaults to 92%. For almost everyone, 92% is the right answer: the JPG is visually identical to the original HEIC for viewing and printing, while staying much smaller than a 100% file.

Lower the quality only when you need a tiny file — for example, a form that caps uploads at a small size. Don't go below 80% for photos you care about; below that, compression artefacts start showing in skies and skin tones. Keep the original HEIC somewhere safe: you can always re-convert from the original, but you can't restore quality lost to a low-quality JPG.

## Troubleshooting: when the conversion fails

The browser route handles almost every iPhone photo, but three hiccups come up:

- **No download appears after converting.** Check the Files app → Downloads. If Safari asks, allow the download — and avoid Private Browsing, which blocks downloads entirely.
- **The converter says the file can't be decoded.** A few HEIC variants (10-bit files, some encoders) can't be decoded in a browser. Export that photo as JPG from the Photos app first (share it to Files, which converts it), or use Preview on a Mac.
- **The file is too big.** The converter accepts files up to 100 MB. A photo that large usually comes from a burst or a long Live Photo — export a still frame from Photos first, then convert that.

If a file fails twice, it's almost always one of these — not the converter.

## The honest limits

Converting HEIC to JPG is a one-way re-encode: the JPG keeps the photo, but it drops the HEIC container's extras, like the Live Photo motion and some depth data. If you love Live Photos, keep the original HEIC in your library and convert only the copies you need to share or upload. And remember that converting doesn't improve a photo — a blurry HEIC becomes an equally blurry JPG, just in a format everyone can open.

## Bottom line

For a single photo, open the [free HEIC to JPG converter](/tools/heic-to-jpg-converter) in Safari and convert it in under a minute — no app, no sign-up, nothing uploaded. If you never want to think about HEIC again, switch your camera to Most Compatible in Settings. Either way, the fix takes less time than the error message did.
